analysis.one_liner: Requires giant corporations to win federal charters, seat employees on boards, and restrict executive stock sales and political spending.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors, was referred to committee in the final weeks of the session, and died without a markup or vote when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require any company with more than $1 billion in annual revenue to obtain a federal corporate charter. Charted companies would have to pursue a public benefit alongside profit, elect employees to at least 40% of their board seats, bar executives from selling company stock for five years and for three years after a share buyback, and get approval from 75% of shareholders and directors before spending money on political campaigns. State attorneys general could petition to revoke the charter of a company that repeatedly engages in serious, illegal misconduct that harms people or communities.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees at large corporations, who would gain board representation and just-cause dismissal protection; everyday investors, who would benefit from executive stock-lockups and a vote on corporate political spending; and the public, which would see a new tool against companies that repeatedly break the law.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and shareholders at giant corporations

how_it_helps.text: Covered employees would elect not less than 2/5 of a corporation's directors, could only be removed from the board for just cause, and would receive the same disclosures shareholders get.

Executives and directors could not sell, transfer, or pledge company stock (or derivatives of it) for five years after acquiring it, or for three years after the company does a Rule 10b-18 share buyback, with civil penalties of one to three times the value of the shares sold.

A corporation could not spend money to support or oppose any federal, state, or local candidate — including payments to outside groups — unless at least 75% of its shareholders and 75% of its directors approved beforehand, and shareholders could sue to block spending that violates the rule.

A state attorney general could petition the new federal Office of United States Corporations to revoke the charter of a corporation that engaged in repeated, egregious, and illegal misconduct causing significant harm, if the company did not fix the causes of the misconduct.
Directors would be required to balance shareholder interests with the interests of employees, customers, suppliers, communities, and the environment, rather than maximizing shareholder value alone.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations with over $1 billion in revenue, which would face a new federal chartering regime, employee board elections, compliance costs, the threat of charter revocation, and limits on executive pay practices and political spending; and their executives and directors, whose stock sales would be restricted.

drawbacks.text: The enforcement of the public-benefit duty is narrow: neither the corporation nor its directors can be held liable for monetary damages for failing to pursue a general public benefit, and only the corporation itself or shareholders holding at least 2% of shares can sue, so ordinary people affected by a company's conduct would have no direct day in court.

Compliance costs would fall on companies with over $1 billion in revenue, and critics of chartering and co-determination schemes argue such costs and legal uncertainty can be passed to consumers and may put U.S. firms at a disadvantage against foreign competitors not bound by the rules.

Giving a federal office the power to revoke a corporation's charter concentrates significant discretionary authority over the legal existence of major companies in the executive branch, which business groups and legal scholars traditionally oppose as a dangerous precedent.

The political-spending approval requirement covers payments to any other person that could be used for electioneering — including dues to trade associations — which could sweep in routine business payments and generate litigation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core gains — employee board representation, executive stock-lockups, and a shareholder veto on campaign spending — would be real for workers and investors, and the costs would be borne almost entirely by very large companies and their executives. But the bill's centerpiece public-benefit duty is weakly enforceable: liability is limited, standing is restricted to the company itself and 2% shareholders, and good-faith business judgments are protected, so critics could fairly say the bill's moral framing outruns its legal teeth. The charter-revocation power is a genuinely far-reaching grant of executive discretion, and opponents' objections to it are not frivolous.

outcome.mechanism: Warren introduced it on December 11, 2024, the Senate read it twice and sent it to the Commerce Committee, and the committee never acted on it before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the Accountable Capitalism Act in the Senate on December 11, 2024, less than a month before the end of the 118th Congress.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day it was introduced.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor — the cosponsor list shows zero members.
The full action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the initial referral; the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations and their executives and directors are better off, because none of the requirements — federal charters, employee board seats, stock-sale lockups, and pre-approval of political spending — will take effect. Workers and small shareholders gain nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Commerce Committee; no other senator joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Sen. Maria Cantwell
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: The committee she chaired received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and only one senator — a Democrat — sponsored the bill with zero cosponsors from either party, so the partisan shape of support or opposition was never measured.

industries.industry: Large U.S. corporations (over $1 billion in gross receipts)
industries.note: The bill would put every corporation above the $1 billion threshold under a new federal chartering regime with employee board elections, a public-benefit duty, campaign-spending pre-approval, and the threat of charter revocation. The companies' interest in avoiding these requirements runs against the workers, investors, and communities the bill would protect.

Covered officers and directors could not sell company stock or derivatives for five years after acquiring them, or for three years after a share buyback, with penalties of one to three times the value of the shares sold. Their financial interest in rapid stock cash-outs is the direct target of the provision.

industries.industry: Corporate political spending and election-advertising industries
industries.note: Any political expenditure over $10,000 per candidate — including payments routed through outside groups or trade associations — would need approval from 75% of shareholders and directors, which would sharply curtail the flow of corporate money into campaigns and the consultants and ad buyers that spend it.

industries.industry: Retail and institutional shareholders of large firms
industries.note: Shareholders would gain a veto over political spending and benefit from executive stock-lockups, but would also absorb compliance costs and bear the litigation burden of enforcing the new duties, since lawsuits are limited to shareholders holding at least 2% of shares.
